notes.meaning: Manasseh took the throne when he was only twelve years old and went on to rule for fifty-five years, the longest reign of any king in Judah. He was born a few years after God healed his father Hezekiah and gave him extra years of life. Young rulers are easily swayed by corrupt advisers, and Manasseh grew up to become Judah's most wicked king.

Manasseh turned Judah back to the very practices God hated and drove out the Canaanites for doing. Idolatry and dark pagan rituals took the place of God's holy law across the kingdom. He completely abandoned the faithful legacy left behind by his father.

Manasseh rebuilt the outdoor shrines his father had torn down and set up altars to the false god Baal. He made a wooden pole for the goddess Asherah, copying the wicked king Ahab of northern Israel. He also began worshiping the sun, moon, and stars, bringing foreign superstitions deep into Judah.

Manasseh went so far as to build pagan altars inside the Lord's temple in Jerusalem. God had chosen that sacred building as the special place for His name to be honored. Setting up idols there was a direct and open insult to the living God.

Manasseh set up altars to worship the sun, moon, and stars in both the outer and inner courtyards of the temple. The sacred courts meant for priests and people to bring offerings to God were turned into stations for star worship. He forced false religion into the heart of God's house.

Manasseh sacrificed his own son by fire, offering him up to the brutal pagan idol Molech. He also plunged into witchcraft, read signs in the clouds, and hired people who claimed to speak with the dead. These dark practices directly defied God's commands and provoked His intense anger.

Manasseh carved a wooden idol of Asherah and placed it right inside the holy temple. God had solemnly promised David and Solomon that Jerusalem and this house would bear His name forever. By putting a pagan idol in that sacred space, the king treated God's special dwelling place with utter contempt.

God had promised that Israel would never be driven from their homeland if they stayed faithful to His laws given through Moses. Their peace and safety always depended on their obedience to God's covenant, which was His solemn agreement with them. By turning their backs on that agreement, the nation put their future in grave danger.

The people refused to listen to God and eagerly followed the king's terrible lead. Because they had God's word and still rejected it, Judah became even more corrupt than the pagan nations God had wiped out before them. Leaders who abuse their influence carry a heavy burden for leading others into sin.

Even when the king and the culture turned their backs on God, the Lord did not remain silent. He sent His messengers, the prophets, to warn the nation about what was coming. These prophets gave the people a clear call to repent before it was too late.

The prophets announced that Manasseh had committed worse sins than the ancient Amorites who lived in the land before Israel. He not only sinned terribly himself, but he also dragged the whole nation of Judah into idolatry. God holds kings and leaders especially responsible when they corrupt their people.

God warned that the disaster coming on Jerusalem and Judah would shock anyone who heard about it. The news would be like a loud, sharp crash that makes the ears ring with terror. The judgment would be so awful that neighboring nations would stand stunned.

God declared He would judge Jerusalem with the exact same strict standard He used when destroying Samaria and Ahab's wicked royal family. He compared the city to a dirty dish that is thoroughly wiped clean and turned upside down to drain. Jerusalem would be emptied of its people and riches, though kept ready to be purified for future use.

God stated He would abandon the remaining tribes of Judah and Benjamin, leaving them without divine protection. Without His defense, they would fall easily to their enemies and be carried off with all their goods. When a people completely cast off God, He eventually leaves them to the consequences of their rebellion.

This judgment was coming because Israel had continually provoked God ever since He brought them out of Egypt. Generation after generation had drifted into idolatry, and Manasseh's reign finally filled the cup of guilt to the brim. God showed great patience over many centuries, but His justice would not wait forever.

Manasseh ruled like a cruel tyrant, slaughtering anyone who stood against his idolatry until Jerusalem was filled with blood. Jewish tradition records that he even murdered the prophet Isaiah by having him sawn in two. The guilt of shedding innocent blood brought an especially heavy cry for divine justice.

The official royal records preserved the details of Manasseh's long reign and the terrible sins he committed. While this account focuses on his wickedness to explain the coming exile, the book of Chronicles later records that he repented after being taken captive to Babylon. God's mercy is great enough to reach even the worst sinners when they humble themselves.

other.label: Orthodox
other.view: An ancient Greek prayer of repentance, known as the Prayer of Manasseh, is preserved in the Septuagint and used in the Orthodox service of Great Compline, though it is not part of the Hebrew Bible.

notes.meaning: Manasseh died and was buried in the garden of his own palace, known as the garden of Uzza, rather than in the historic royal tombs of David. He may have chosen this private garden burial out of genuine humility, feeling unworthy to rest beside the faithful kings before him. His son Amon then took over the throne.

Amon became king at twenty-two years old, but his reign lasted only two short years in Jerusalem. He followed the short-lived pattern of several sons of wicked kings who died quickly after taking power. His mother was Meshullemeth, who came from the Judean town of Jotbah.

Amon committed evil just as his father Manasseh had done in the worst days of his reign. He embraced idolatry and rejected the true worship of God. He copied his father's wicked actions while completely ignoring his father's later repentance.

Amon walked in every sinful path of his father and gave his worship to the very same pagan idols. Even though Manasseh had torn down idols late in life, Amon revived those corrupt practices. Setting a bad example often leads children into deep sin that parents cannot undo later.

Amon completely deserted the Lord, the God of his ancestors, and refused to obey His commandments. He showed no desire to follow God's law or reform the kingdom. His short life was defined by total disloyalty to the Lord.

After only two years on the throne, Amon's own palace officials plotted against him and murdered him in his home. His own house, which should have protected him, became the place of his death. God allowed this unfaithful king's life to be cut short in his sins.

The common people of Judah rose up, executed the conspirators who had murdered the king, and placed Amon's eight-year-old son Josiah on the throne. By doing this, the people avenged the unlawful assassination and kept God's promised royal family line intact. This tragic moment paved the way for one of Judah's most godly kings.

The remainder of Amon's brief reign and his public deeds were recorded in the official chronicles of Judah's kings. His life was brief and shameful, leaving behind no good deeds to remember. His record stands as a solemn warning against persistent rebellion.

Amon was buried in the family tomb in the garden of Uzza, right next to his father Manasseh. His young son Josiah succeeded him, marking a dramatic turning point from wickedness back toward God. Even in dark times, God preserved His promises and raised up a godly leader for His people.
